 Repairing Instead of Demolishing: Architects Hold Workshop on Homes Damaged by the Kumamoto Earthquake
 18/11/2026
 Emergency Support 
 Japan 
 From October 31 to November 2, AAR Japan (Association for Aid and Relief, Japan) held a series of workshops in Uki City, Yatsushiro City, and Hikawa Town in Kumamoto Prefecture to help earthquake survivors learn about options for repairing damaged homes. Twenty-six participants, including homeowners whose houses were damaged by the earthquake, attended the sessions and learned about the benefits of repairing their homes rather than demolishing and rebuilding them, as well as available public support programs.
 Participants learn about options for repairing earthquake-damaged homes in Uki city, Kumamoto Prefecture on October 31, 2026
 Considering Alternatives to Demolition
 More than three months have passed since the earthquake. As of November 4, 2,807 homes in Kumamoto Prefecture had been officially classified as completely destroyed, while 10,463 had been classified as severely damagedLocal governments have begun accepting applications for the public demolition program, a government-funded program that removes disaster-damaged homes at no cost to owners, for houses assessed as severely damaged or worse. In Uki City, Yatsushiro City, and Hikawa Town, applications are being accepted through the end of March next year.At the same time, opportunities remain limited for homeowners to seek advice on whether their houses can be repaired, what repairs might cost, and what public assistance may be available.
 The workshops were led by architect and housing preservation specialist Mr.Hasegawa, representative of the Housing Repair Support Network. He has supported the repair and preservation of homes and historic buildings in disaster-affected areas across Japan, including after the Niigata Chuetsu Earthquake, the Great East Japan Earthquake, the 2016 Kumamoto Earthquake, and the Noto Peninsula Earthquake.Drawing on lessons learned from past disasters, Mr.Hasegawa introduced recovery options beyond demolition and rebuilding and shared examples of how damaged homes can be successfully repaired.
 Architect Mr. Hasegawa explaining at the workshop in Yatsushiro city on November 1
 Exploring the Benefits of Repair
 During the workshops, participants learned how repairing homes where families have lived for many years can help people return to their daily lives more quickly while remaining connected to their communities. Repairing homes can also preserve places that hold important family memories and, in some cases, reduce the financial burden compared with rebuilding. Mr.Hasegawa encouraged participants not to rush into major decisions while still coping with the uncertainty that follows a disaster.
 The workshops also highlighted how preserving existing homes can help maintain local communities and reduce disaster-related waste.Many participants had assumed that public demolition was their only option. Some commented, “My home was classified as completely destroyed, but I would like to know whether repairs are still possible,” while others said, “I would like an architect to assess my home before deciding what to do.”
 By learning about repair options and available support programs, participants are now better equipped to make informed decisions about rebuilding their homes. We will continue providing disaster survivors with the information and assistance they need as recovery efforts move forward. We sincerely ask for your support for AAR’s assistance to people affected by the Kumamoto Earthquake.
